articles.title: In November 2015, a cat called Meeko was discovered around half a mile (about 800 metres) from the damaged facility, after surviving alone for around four and a half years
articles.summary: Discover the extraordinary story of Meeko, a cat who survived alone for 4½ years in the Fukushima exclusion zone after the 2011 nuclear disaster. Her incredible resilience and the ongoing efforts of rescue groups highlight the challenges faced by abandoned animals.
articles.body: People find it difficult enough to leave their homes quickly. For pets, it can mean being abandoned with no one to feed them and no indication of when someone will return. This is what happened to many dogs and cats near the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear facility during the March 2011 accident, and it sets the stage for one of the most amazing animal survival stories to emerge from the exclusion zone. In November 2015, a cat called Meeko was discovered around half a mile (about 800 metres) from the damaged facility, after surviving on her own for around four and a half years. SPCA International, a nonprofit animal welfare group that supports the rescue organisation Animal Rescue Nyander Guard, describes her survival as miraculous. It says Meeko now lives in a foster home nearby that also serves as a cat café.Why pets were left behindThe trouble began with a magnitude 9.0 earthquake in March 2011 that triggered meltdowns at three of the four reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi plant. People who lived near the plant were evacuated, but companion animals and cattle remained where they were. In the weeks that followed, Fukushima prefectural authorities began searching for pets inside the no entry zone, a 20 kilometre radius around the plant, the Asahi Shimbun later reported.Prefectural officials later described the scope of that search to the Asahi Shimbun. They said 463 dogs and 545 cats had been captured and kept at a shelter over four years and eight months. About 30% were returned to their owners, about 60% found new homes, and the remainder died in the shelter. In December 2015, the prefecture closed the shelter, concluding that it was highly unlikely any pets remained in the restricted area. That Meeko was found only weeks before the closure shows how hard it was to account for every animal.How rare survival wasMayumi Itoh, a former political science professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, examined the animals’ fate in her 2018 book Animals and the Fukushima Nuclear Disaster, published by Palgrave Macmillan. The publisher’s description says about 100,000 residents were evacuated from the 20-kilometre zone while companion animals and livestock were left behind, and that about 90% of the animals in the zone died. It calls the book the first comprehensive english-language study of those animals, and it sets the government’s policy against the work of volunteer groups that filled the gap.Against that figure, Meeko’s four and a half years stand out. She survived four winters and nearly the full length of the prefecture’s capture programme before anyone found her. SPCA International’s statement does not explain how she found food and shelter, and it does not say whether she had any outside help, such as the feeding sites that rescue groups maintain in the zone. It says only that she lived on her own. What is clear is the time frame and the distance. No one expected to find a cat living half a mile from a plant that had suffered three meltdowns. Her rescue also sits inside a longer effort that did not end when the shelter did.Rescue work that goes onAnimal Rescue Nyander Guard provides medical care to rescued animals, reunites families with their pets and finds new homes for cats and dogs, SPCA International said. Dogs that live in heavily radiated areas and cannot be removed are monitored and cared for there throughout the year. The feeding points in the exclusion zone use boxes set up high with small entrances, so larger wild animals cannot reach the food. A dog named Piccolo had been living on his own in the zone for over six years, though Nyander Guard made regular trips to feed him and look after his health.Some of these stories end happily. A cat called Dot, rescued in 2013, stayed at the Nyander Guard shelter until June 2016, when her owner was reunited with her after his daughter found a photo of the cat online and contacted the group. They had been apart for five years. Others were never given the chance. Love, a cat, lived in the exclusion zone for six years and died alone in August 2017, SPCA International says. Her owner had hoped to return home, but radiation levels were too high.Some have opted to stay and care for the animals themselves. Sakae Kato, who used to manage a small construction firm, told Reuters in 2021 that he was caring for 41 cats in his home in Namie and an empty structure on his land and had buried another 23 in his garden. Meeko’s story comes down to a few facts. She was rescued about half a mile from the Fukushima Daiichi plant in November 2015, after surviving on her own for almost four and a half years, and she now lives in a foster home that doubles as a cat café. Her survival stands out in a zone where, according to Itoh’s book, about 90% of the animals died, and her rescue shows why private groups kept searching after the prefecture closed its shelter.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Papa, mai maa ke pass ja rha hu': Jhansi teen records video, shoots himself with pistol
articles.summary: JHANSI: A 19-year-old BA student allegedly died by suicide using his father’s licensed pistol at their home in the Gursarai police station area of Uttar
articles.body: JHANSI: A 19-year-old BA student allegedly died by suicide using his father’s licensed pistol at their home in the Gursarai police station area of Uttar Pradesh’s Jhansi district on Sunday morning.Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death after recovering a video he recorded on his mobile phone shortly before the incident.The deceased, Love Patel, was the only child of Munna Lal Patel, a retired village development officer who now works in agriculture.Love was found lying inside a room with a gunshot wound after neighbours alerted his family on hearing a gunshot. He was rushed to the Community Health Centre in Gursarai, where doctors declared him dead.Around 8am on Sunday, Munna Lal and his wife, Hemlata, left for the fields, leaving Love alone at home. Around two hours later, neighbours heard a gunshot and rushed to the house but found the door locked from inside.They alerted Munna Lal, who returned and found his son lying on the floor with a gunshot wound. His licensed pistol was found nearby.Police reached the spot and launched an investigation. A forensic team collected evidence, and the body was sent for a post-mortem examination.Video recovered from mobile phoneThe video recorded by Love shortly before his death has become a key part of the investigation. In the recording, he reportedly addresses his father emotionally, saying he had caused him considerable distress and continued to trouble him.He then turns the camera towards a photograph of his mother and says, “Papa, paise apne paas rakho, ab mai maa ke paas ja raha hoon” (Dad, keep the money with you. I am going to be with my mother).He reportedly says he does not hold his friends, family members or relatives responsible for his decision.Police are examining the recording and other evidence to establish the circumstances surrounding his death. The reason remains unclear.Father says son was under stressDuring questioning, Munna Lal reportedly told police that Love often remained under stress and had difficulty sleeping at night. He said his son sometimes took medication to help him sleep. Police are examining these details, but no cause has been established.Love’s mother, Sangeeta Patel, died by suicide after setting herself on fire in 2009. Love had been living with his father since her death. According to the family, Munna Lal had married Hemlata before marrying Sangeeta, with whom he had Love.Police investigation underwayGarotha Circle Officer Piyush Kumar Pandey said Love was a resident of Singar village and was pursuing a BA degree.According to the officer, preliminary information indicates that Love locked himself inside a room and shot himself with his father’s licensed pistol. His family took him to the hospital, where doctors declared him dead.Police have questioned Munna Lal, while the forensic team has examined the scene and collected evidence. articles.title: Who named Cyclone Arnab and why? Where it will hit, states on alert and preparedness
articles.summary: India is bracing for Cyclone Arnab as it moves towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, with landfall expected by Wednesday forenoon as authorities expect strong
articles.body: India is bracing for Cyclone Arnab as it moves towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, with landfall expected by Wednesday forenoon as authorities expect strong winds, heavy rainfall and possible flooding across several states.Cyclone Arnab is drawing attention not only for its projected impact along the Andhra Pradesh coast but also for its name.Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast maximum sustained wind speeds of 115-125 kmph, with gusts reaching 140 kmph, when the storm crosses the coast near Yanam, between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam. Its effects are expected in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, prompting weather alerts and precautionary measures.Why is it named Arnab? How storm naming worksThe name Arnab was contributed by Bangladesh to the list of names used for tropical cyclones over the North Indian Ocean. It is pronounced “Ornab”.Cyclone names in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea are assigned by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO)/United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) Panel on Tropical Cyclones. The naming system began in 2004, with the list subsequently expanded as more countries joined the panel.The current list contains 52 names contributed by 13 countries: Bangladesh, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. The list was adopted in April 2020.Names are used sequentially, column-wise, according to the established list. Each name is used only once and is not repeated in subsequent lists. The Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre in New Delhi, operated by the IMD, is responsible for naming cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea once they reach the prescribed intensity.Naming storms helps meteorological agencies, governments, disaster management authorities and the public identify and communicate warnings about individual weather systems more easily.Andhra Pradesh braces for landfallThe cyclone was centred over the west-central Bay of Bengal on Tuesday morning, moving west-northwestwards before its expected turn towards the coast. The Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) has warned of heavy rainfall in northern coastal districts, including Srikakulam, with strong winds already affecting parts of the coast.Authorities have identified 16 districts, covering 2,460 revenue villages and 92 urban areas, as potentially vulnerable. According to the state disaster management authorities, 1,763 cyclone shelters have been readied, 2,907 control rooms established and 3,185 nodal officers deployed. National and state disaster response teams have also been positioned in 11 high-risk districts.Authorities have banned public access to beaches and announced restrictions on coastal road movement. Fishing vessels have been secured at harbours, with the APSDMA saying 30,043 fishing vessels have been anchored.Air India has warned that adverse weather could affect flights to and from Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada on October 27. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status and allow additional time for travel to airports.Odisha, Jharkhand face heavy rain, strong windsOdisha has already experienced heavy rain and strong winds in parts of the state. The IMD has issued an orange warning for heavy to very heavy rainfall, ranging from 12 cm to 20 cm, in Puri, Gajapati, Ganjam, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri. A yellow warning has been issued for several other districts.Tourist boat and ferry operations at Chilika Lake have been suspended from October 26 to 29 as a precaution. Authorities have moved boats to safer locations, while Paradip Port has provided shelter to 305 fishermen at its Eastern Quay-1 berth.In Jharkhand, the state government has directed district administrations to remain vigilant. A yellow alert for heavy rain has been issued for several districts on October 28, followed by orange alerts for parts of the state through October 30. Thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds are also expected.The Ranchi district administration has warned of waterlogging, overflowing drains and water bodies, damage to weak structures and possible flood-like conditions in low-lying areas. Standing crops could also be affected by water accumulation.West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh also likely to see unseasonal rainThe cyclone's influence is expected to extend to West Bengal between October 28 and 30. In south Bengal, heavy rainfall is forecast in South 24 Parganas, Purba Medinipur, Paschim Medinipur, Jhargram, Purulia, Bankura and Paschim Bardhaman on October 28 and 29. Kolkata is likely to receive light to moderate rain over the next 48 hours.In the sub-Himalayan region, Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Alipurduar and Jalpaiguri are likely to experience heavy rain on October 29 and 30. The IMD has also advised fishermen not to venture into the sea until October 29, warning of rough to very rough conditions and squally winds of 40-50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph, along and off the West Bengal coast.Uttar Pradesh is forecast to receive unseasonal rain, thunderstorms and strong winds between October 28 and 31. The IMD has issued alerts for several districts, with heavy rain possible in parts of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Awadh and the Terai region. Daytime temperatures could fall by 5-8 degrees Celsius in some areas on October 30.Authorities have advised residents to follow official weather bulletins, avoid unnecessary travel during storms and stay away from trees, electricity poles, weak structures and open fields during lightning.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: KALYAN: More than a month after a 22-year-old married woman accused former BJP MLA Narendra Pawar and dismissed police constable Shailesh Patil of gang-raping her at a farmhouse in Bhiwandi taluka, the Congress has questioned the police investigation, alleging that the accused are being shielded.Kanchan Kulkarni, Congress group leader in the Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation (KDMC) who had helped victim to get FIR registered in this case, has accused the police of inaction and questioned why the two accused have not been arrested despite the seriousness of the allegations.She alleged that the police were extending help to the accused and demanded accountability over the delay in their arrest.The case was registered at Padgha police station in September following a complaint by the woman, who alleged that Pawar had called her to his office on the pretext of helping resolve a dispute with her husband.According to the FIR, she was subsequently taken to a farmhouse in Bapgaon, where Pawar and Patil allegedly sexually assaulted her. The complaint also mentions the alleged use of a firearm to threaten her.Senior inspector Pankaj Giri of Padgha police station said six police teams had been deployed to trace the accused. Search operations were also being conducted at railway stations and airports, according to information provided by the police.Kulkarni questioned the delay in the arrests, arguing that the police act swiftly against ordinary citizens but have yet to apprehend the accused in this case. Her allegations have brought the pace of the investigation under renewed scrutiny.Meanwhile, the Bhiwandi additional sessions court had rejected Pawar's anticipatory bail application on September 28.The court observed that the allegations were serious, that a prima facie case had been made out and that custodial interrogation was necessary for an effective investigation.With both accused yet to be arrested, the focus is now on the police's efforts to trace them and the progress of the investigation amid the Congress's allegations of inaction.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: London's Natural History Museum won a landmark legal fight to reduce its annual rental value from £12.92 million to just £1; the decision could reshape how national museums are taxed
articles.summary: London’s Natural History Museum has won a landmark legal challenge that reduced its rateable value for business rates from £12.92 million to just £1,
articles.body: London’s Natural History Museum has won a landmark legal challenge that reduced its rateable value for business rates from £12.92 million to just £1, marking a significant development for publicly funded cultural institutions across England. The Valuation Tribunal for England ruled that the museum should not be assessed as though it were a profitable commercial property, given its financial position and commitment to free public admission. The decision has since prompted a change in the government’s approach to valuing free-entry museums and galleries, potentially bringing substantial financial relief to institutions facing rising operating costs.The Natural History Museum won its landmark business rates challengeThe Natural History Museum’s successful appeal centred on how its property should be valued for business rates. According to the Museums Association, the museum was initially assigned a rateable value of £12.92 million in the 2017 Rating List. This was subsequently reduced to £4.16 million using a method based on the estimated cost of rebuilding the property. The museum challenged that assessment, arguing that a nominal valuation of £1 better reflected the economic realities of operating the institution.The Valuation Tribunal for England heard the case over two days in February 2026 and issued its decision in March. The ruling established that the museum’s rateable value should be reduced to £1, effective from 1 April 2017. The initial work on appealing the decision was subsequently abandoned, allowing the judgment to stand.As explained by law firm Mills & Reeve in its analysis of the ruling, the tribunal considered whether the museum could realistically be operated profitably by a hypothetical tenant. Its findings supported the museum’s argument that its specialist buildings, collections and public-service responsibilities made it fundamentally different from an ordinary commercial property.The decision was particularly significant because the museum became the first national museum in the UK to win such a business rates challenge.Why was the museum considered unsuitable for commercial valuationThe tribunal’s decision rested on the distinction between a commercial property and an institution whose primary purpose is public service. The Natural History Museum preserves and displays collections, conducts scientific research and provides free access to visitors. Its operations are not designed to generate the profits expected from a conventional commercial enterprise.Mills & Reeve explained that the museum’s financial accounts demonstrated that it could not operate profitably, even with government grant funding. The tribunal also concluded that there was no realistic prospect of a commercially motivated organisation taking on the building under the same conditions.The valuation dispute involved the receipts and expenditure method, which examines an organisation’s income and operating costs to determine the rent a hypothetical tenant might reasonably pay. The tribunal accepted that this was the appropriate approach for the museum.However, the assessment could not rely on speculative income that the institution did not actually receive. The government funding provided to the museum was conditional on free public admission and could not simply be treated as rental income available to a hypothetical commercial tenant.The tribunal also declined to give decisive weight to hypothetical admission charges and other assumptions about how the museum might operate differently. Its actual financial performance provided a more reliable basis for determining the property’s value.Importance of this ruling for other museumsThe implications extend well beyond the Natural History Museum. According to the Museums Association, free-entry museums and galleries across England are expected to benefit from a change in the way their business rates valuations are calculated.Following the tribunal decision, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport confirmed that the Valuation Office would stop using the notional receipts approach when assessing free-entry museums where that method had previously been applied.Under the earlier approach, assessors could estimate hypothetical ticket revenue by considering visitor numbers and an assumed admission charge, even when the museum offered free entry. For institutions that depend heavily on public funding and have limited income from other sources, these calculations could produce valuations that did not reflect their actual financial circumstances.The October report explained that the government’s revised approach followed the tribunal’s rejection of notional receipts in the Natural History Museum case. HM Revenue and Customs confirmed that the change in rating case law would need to be reflected across the museums and art galleries sector where the approach had been used.Several museums had already established relevant legal precedents. These included Exeter’s Royal Albert Memorial Museum, Tyne and Wear Archives and Museums, now known as North East Museums, and York Museum and Gallery Trust. The Natural History Museum’s victory extended this line of decisions to a major national institution.How could the decision ease financial pressure on cultural institutionsThe revised valuation approach could help museums redirect money previously allocated to business rates towards their core responsibilities. Maintaining historic buildings, caring for collections, conducting research and providing public access all require substantial resources.The Museums Association highlighted the potential for significant backdated savings for the Natural History Museum following the reduction in its valuation. The decision could also provide other museums and public bodies with grounds to review their own business rates liabilities.However, a reduction to £1 is not guaranteed for every institution. The Museums Association noted that HMRC expects some museums to retain higher valuations where their receipts and expenditure demonstrate a surplus.The Valuation Office will also consider reliable rental evidence where it is available, as this is regarded as a more accurate indicator of a property's rateable value.You use AI every day. articles.title: Five years after Rangers manager Walter Smith died, his widow Ethel chose the cancer unit that treated him to receive £50,000 from a charity, one of the biggest donations in the Scottish hospital's history
articles.summary: Five years after former Rangers and Scotland manager Walter Smith died following a battle with cancer, his widow Ethel has chosen to honour his memory by
articles.body: Five years after former Rangers and Scotland manager Walter Smith died following a battle with cancer, his widow Ethel has chosen to honour his memory by directing a £50,000 charitable donation to the hospital unit that cared for him. The gift, made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation, was presented to the cancer unit at Vale of Leven Hospital in Alexandria, Scotland, on October 26, 2026, the fifth anniversary of his death.According to STV News, Ethel nominated the unit in recognition of the treatment and support her husband received there. The donation is among the largest the hospital has received and will be used to improve facilities and make treatment more comfortable for patients. Hospital officials said the exact plans for spending the money were still being determined when the gift was announced.“When I was asked where I would like the money to go, I had no hesitation in nominating the unit here at the Vale,” Ethel said, explaining that the family wanted to acknowledge the care provided by the hospital. “Walter received treatment here, so it felt fitting as a thank you for the care we received from the unit and the hospital in general,” she added.The donation was formally presented to June Raines, the unit's charge nurse, and Gerry O'Hare, a former clinical nurse specialist who cared for Smith during his treatment. The contribution will support the unit's work serving patients from across the surrounding region.Cancer unit that cared for Walter SmithVale of Leven Hospital is located in Alexandria, West Dunbartonshire, and provides cancer treatment and other services to patients in the west of Scotland. Its haematology-oncology unit offers day-care treatment, allowing many patients to receive care close to home without requiring an overnight hospital stay. According to Scottish News, the unit has 12 treatment chairs and a phlebotomy service. Its treatments and support include chemotherapy, blood transfusions and symptom management for people with cancer and blood disorders.For the Smith family, the hospital's importance went beyond its medical services. Ethel's decision to nominate the unit reflected the personal experience of receiving care during a difficult period. Gerry O'Hare, who now works part-time at the Beatson in Glasgow, said the donation would help support a service that had meant a great deal to Smith and his family.“Having worked at the Vale and knowing personally how much the unit meant to Walter and his family, it is wonderful to see such a significant donation coming back to support its patients,” O'Hare said, according to STV News. He added that the service was important to the local community and welcomed the foundation's contribution towards its continued work.June Raines also thanked the foundation, noting that the unit's ability to provide treatment locally helped patients avoid travelling farther for care. She said the funding would allow the hospital to enhance its facilities and improve the experience of people coming in for treatment.A charity established after a personal lossThe donation was made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation, established by businessman Andy Smillie after his daughter died from cancer. The foundation raises money to support cancer services across Scotland through charitable contributions and fundraising activities.The latest gift is not the first time the organisation has supported Vale of Leven Hospital. STV News reported that the foundation had made a similar £50,000 donation to the hospital around four years earlier.The new contribution brings together two families' experiences of cancer and loss. The foundation was established in memory of Smillie's daughter, while Ethel's nomination reflects the care her husband received during his illness.The funding will be used to improve the hospital unit's facilities and patient experience, although the precise projects to be supported have not yet been announced. The hospital's leadership welcomed the donation, saying it would help staff continue providing compassionate care to patients and their families.Rebecca Reid, interim director for NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde's Clyde Sector, thanked the foundation and Ethel for selecting the hospital. She said the money would help the unit improve the experience of patients receiving treatment at Vale of Leven.Walter Smith's legacy beyond footballSmith died aged 73 on October 26, 2021, following a battle with cancer. He remains one of the most respected figures in Scottish football, particularly for his achievements with Rangers, where he enjoyed two successful spells as manager. During his first spell at Ibrox, Smith won 13 major trophies in seven years before becoming Scotland manager in December 2004. He returned to Rangers in 2007 and added another eight trophies before retiring in 2011 after completing a domestic double.He also managed Everton and led Scotland's national team for three years. His achievements made him a defining figure in Rangers' modern history, while his influence extended to players and fellow managers who worked with him.The donation arrives as supporters and the club continue to remember Smith five years after his death. However, its significance lies not only in the football manager's legacy but also in the practical support it will provide to people receiving cancer treatment.By nominating the unit that cared for her husband, Ethel has ensured that the family's gratitude will translate into support for other patients facing similar challenges. The £50,000 contribution will help the hospital improve its facilities and treatment environment, allowing Smith's memory to be associated with care for the community as well as his achievements on the pitch.You use AI every day. articles.title: TOI Youth Icons Summit: Para-badminton champ Suhas says youth should aim to rank among top 5% in their fields
articles.summary: Para-badminton champion and IAS officer Suhas Lalinakere Yathiraj addressed young achievers and emerging leaders at the TOI Youth Icons Summit & Awards –
articles.body: Para-badminton champion and IAS officer Suhas Lalinakere Yathiraj addressed young achievers and emerging leaders at the TOI Youth Icons Summit & Awards – UP Chapter in Lucknow on Tuesday, sharing lessons from his journey in sports and public service and urging young people to strive for excellence in their chosen fields.Speaking at the summit, Suhas emphasised the importance of taking the first step towards one's goals, despite the fear of failure and concerns about societal judgement. “First step, the most difficult because we think what people and society will think if we lose,” he said.Sharing his approach to success, the badminton champion said, “I have a thumb rule which I believe most of the successful people here have too, Whatever stream you are in, aim to reach the top 5 per cent of that particular stream, if you become a lawyer become the best one, if doctor become the best…whatever field you choose…Can you make it to the top 5 per cent of the pyramid.”He also spoke about the importance of perseverance, noting that setbacks are an inevitable part of life. “Ups and downs will always be a part of life, Just like the stock market. But just as the stock market, you will be successful in the long term,” he said.Encouraging young people to take chances rather than live with regret, the para-athlete said, “Its better to try and fail, than to not try at all and regret as you grow old.”He also cautioned against complacency after achieving success. “Remember it is easier to reach the peak than to stay there consistently; the enemy of success is complacency so we should not be complacent in any case,” he said.The TOI Youth Icons Summit & Awards – UP Chapter brought together achievers, emerging leaders and influential voices to celebrate young Indians shaping the country's future. The awards recognised outstanding achievers from Uttar Pradesh across categories including enterprise, sports, society, culture and social media.The summit also featured discussions on Uttar Pradesh's transformation over the years, including improvements in job opportunities for young people, safety and connectivity. The event focused on recognising young people whose ambition, ideas and achievements are contributing to India's future.Addressing the issue of addiction among young people, Suhas called it a rising problem and stressed the need to recognise the consequences of one's actions. “Addiction amomg youth is rising problem, we must realise that every action has consequences, so does addiction,” he said.Suhas is an Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer and para-badminton player. He has won silver medals at the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Paralympic Games and gold at the 2024 BWF Para Badminton World Championships.
